«Быстроупак».finding: An invented NEP-era trade name in Ilf and Petrov's Twelve Chairs (1928), formed by compressing быстро ('fast') + упак(овка) ('packing'). It is the packing/wrapping firm owned by Dyadyev, one of the Stargorod conspirators of the 'Union of Sword and Ploughshare' and a mark for the scam; the narration names him 'the owner of Bystroupak'. The coinage parodies the clipped, telescoped commercial and bureaucratic names of the 1920s Soviet economy, so a period reader heard it as a comic private-trader brand, not a surname. The established public-domain English translation renders it as the single compressed word 'Fastpack', which reproduces that quick+pack telescoping.
«Быстроупак».note_for_reader: Coined NEP trade name (Russian bystro 'fast' + upak- 'packing'), in the clipped style of 1920s Soviet firms.
«Быстроупак».rationale: I keep denotation (a packing firm) and connotation/register (a telescoped period business coinage that reads as a brand, not a name) by mimicking the quick+pack compounding in each language; I give up the Russian sound 'Bystro-', since transliterating it would read as a foreign proper noun and force a footnote.

Старкомхоз.finding: Старкомхоз is a telescoped Soviet acronym for the Старгородский комхоз — the Stargorod коммунальное хозяйство, i.e. the town's communal/municipal-services board handling utilities, roads, housing and sanitation. In the tram chapter Treukhov drudges in its отдел благоустройства ('paving department'), and Gavrilin, freshly transferred from Samarkand, is its new заведующий ('head'), later chairman of the gubispolkom, who eventually champions the tramway. To a 1928 reader the word was instantly legible NEP-era officialese: the kind of clipped bureaucratic compound (Star- + kom- + khoz) that the narrators cite deadpan, its very form a small joke about Soviet acronym-mania.

Старкомхоз.note_for_reader: Starkomkhoz = clipped Soviet acronym for the Stargorod communal-services board; Gavrilin is its head.
Старкомхоз.rationale: Keeps denotation (the municipal communal-services authority, so 'head/chairman of ___' reads naturally) and institutional register; gives up the comic compression of the coined acronym, kept only as a trace via the parenthetical 'Starkomkhoz' in English.

Старгород.finding: Старгород is the fictional provincial town where Bender and Vorobyaninov's chase begins in Part One of The Twelve Chairs. The name is transparent to a Russian reader: стар- (from старый, 'old') + город ('town'), so it reads as a generic 'Old-town', the archetypal sleepy pre-revolutionary provincial city. Ilf and Petrov did not coin it; it is borrowed from Leskov's chronicle Соборяне (Cathedral Folk), where Старгород already stands for old-world, patriarchal, church-bound provincial Russia, giving the NEP-era satire an ironic backdrop of faded gentility. It denotes no real place (loosely evoking towns like Oryol) and functions as an 'Anytown' of the old order. Existing English (Fisher, and the classic lib.ru translation), Japanese (Egawa Taku's 十二の椅子) and Chinese editions all transliterate it rather than translate the meaning.
Старгород.note_for_reader: Stargorod = 'Old-town' (Russian star-/old + gorod/town); a fictional archetypal provincial city, borrowed from Leskov.
Старгород.rationale: All three bind the established transliteration, keeping denotation and the proper-name register so the town reads consistently across editions; the 'old town' connotation is given up in the text and restored by a one-line note.

Паша Эмильевич.finding: Minor character in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928), introduced in the chapter 'Голубой воришка' (The Blue/Bashful Thief). He is a young, strapping relative (свояк) and hanger-on of Alkhen (Alexander Yakovlevich), the embezzling director of the Second Stargorod Home for the Aged; he is famous for gluttony (eating two kilograms of tyulka fish or Alkhen's whole ration of sugar at a sitting) and does the manual work of the household's petty thieving, here hauling the barrow of goods. The narration refers to him as 'Паша', the coarser diminutive 'Пашка', and by full name+patronymic 'Паша Эмильевич'; the mismatch of the folksy Russian pet-name 'Паша' (from Павел/Paul) with the foreign-flavored patronymic 'Эмильевич' (from Эмиль/Emil) gives the name a faintly comic, petty-crook ring. There is no scholarly dispute over the referent; the only real task is fixing one canonical spelling and keeping its diminutives linked.

Паша Эмильевич.note_for_reader: Pasha/Pashka are diminutives of the same man; the odd pet-name-plus-patronymic sounds mildly comic in Russian.
Паша Эмильевич.rationale: Kept denotation and the register-neutral proper-name form across all three, transliterating consistently so Pasha, Pashka and the full name stay recognizably one person; gave up the built-in comic incongruity of a Russian nickname wedded to a foreign patronymic, which transliteration cannot carry.

«Титаник».finding: «Титаник» is the brand name of a cheap hair dye Vorobyaninov buys at the chemist's (confiscated contraband) to darken his grey hair and moustache; instead of black it turns him green, and a second dye layered over it leaves a rainbow, forcing him to shave bald. The name is simply the ship Titanic (Russian Титаник), and the joke is the omen: a product named after the century's most famous disaster performs like one. The chapter title «Следы «Титаника»» ('Traces of the Titanic') puns on the wreck's traces and the dye's traces on his skull. Existing English translations keep the brand as 'Titanic'; the ship's name is standardly 泰坦尼克 in Chinese and タイタニック in Japanese, so the disaster connotation survives untranslated in every target.
«Титаник».rationale: Kept the brand as the globally known ship name, preserving denotation and the disaster/omen connotation that drives the chapter-title pun; gave up nothing beyond adding 'hair dye/染发剂/染毛剤' on first mention so the reader sees it is a product, not the ship.

2-й дом Старсобеса.finding: In Ilf and Petrov's Двенадцать стульев the 2-й дом Старсобеса is a state old-people's home occupying Vorobyaninov's former mansion in Stargorod, run by the 'shy little thief' Alexander Yakovlevich (Alchen). 'Старсобес' compresses Старгородский собес — the Stargorod social-security/welfare department (собес = отдел социального обеспечения) — and the numbered '2nd Home' is part of the joke: the name parodies the flood of clipped Soviet bureaucratic acronyms of the 1920s NEP years. To a Russian reader it reads as deadpan officialese, an imposing bureaucratic label over a shabby, corruptly run almshouse. The classic Richardson English translation renders the signboard 'SECOND SOCIAL SECURITY HOME OF THE STAR-PROV-INS-AD' to mimic the acronym; Anne Fisher's 2011 version uses 'Second Stargorod Social Security Home.'

2-й дом Старсобеса.note_for_reader: 'Starsobes' is a clipped Soviet-style acronym for the Stargorod social-security dept; the pompous name masks a shabby, thief-run almshouse.
2-й дом Старсобеса.rationale: Kept denotation and the dry officialese register in all three; gave up the compressed-acronym wordplay of 'Старсобес' (only Richardson's invented 'STAR-PROV-INS-AD' reproduces it), recovering that connotation in the note.

Ипполит Матвеевич.finding: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov is the co-protagonist of Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928): a former marshal of the nobility reduced under Soviet rule to a registrar of births, marriages and deaths in a provincial town, who joins con man Ostap Bender to hunt jewels sewn into one of twelve dining chairs. The full name is grand and pre-revolutionary, and the comedy repeatedly deflates it: Bender rarely uses it, calling him instead the childish pet-name 'Kisa' ('Pussy/Kitty'). Standard English editions (e.g. Fisher; Aplin) keep 'Ippolit Matveyevich'; established Chinese editions use 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 (surname 沃洛比亚尼诺夫); Japanese coverage uses イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ.

Ипполит Матвеевич.note_for_reader: Ostap addresses him by the mock-affectionate nickname Kisa ('Pussycat'), deflating this grand name.
Ипполит Матвеевич.rationale: Standard transliterations preserve denotation and the pompous pre-revolutionary register; the joke of the name's grandeur versus his ruined station carries only through context and the Kisa contrast, which no transliteration alone conveys.

Елена Станиславовна.finding: Elena Stanislavovna Bour is a minor character in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928): a former prosecutor's widow and one-time mistress of Vorobyaninov, now scraping by in Stargorod as a card-reading fortune-teller with a parrot. In chapter X (The Mechanic, the Parrot and the Fortune-Teller) her flat hosts the meeting of the bogus conspiracy the Union of the Sword and Ploughshare. On the cited pages she appears by first name and patronymic only; her surname Boure is given elsewhere, so the patronymic pairing Елена Станиславовна is the stable form to keep. The full Russian first-name-plus-patronymic is a respectful, slightly old-regime form of address that also marks her as a faded gentlewoman clinging to former status.

Елена Станиславовна.note_for_reader: Russian given name + patronymic (father Stanislav); a polite, faintly old-fashioned way of naming her.
Елена Станиславовна.rationale: Kept denotation and the formal first-name/patronymic register through standard transliteration in each language; gave up the connotation that this address form flags a genteel has-been, which no transliteration carries.

Гусище.finding: Гусище is a fictional toponym in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928): the poor outlying district of Stargorod where the archivist Varfolomei Korobeinikov lives. The text places it by the railway embankment, inhabited mainly by railwaymen, a scatter of huts (халупы) and temporary barracks among long, still-damp brick cooperative blocks. The name is built from гусь ('goose') plus the augmentative-pejorative suffix -ище, so a 1920s Russian reader heard a folksy, slightly squalid nickname — a 'Gooseton'/'Goose-slum' on the wrong side of the tracks — not a dignified street name. It is a coined place name, not a real Stargorod (itself invented), and carries the deadpan comic register of the surrounding narration.
Гусище.note_for_reader: Gusishche: a made-up district name from Russian gus ('goose') plus a pejorative suffix — a scruffy railway-workers' edge of town.
Гусище.rationale: All three keep the term as a proper place name by transliteration, preserving denotation and its status as a toponym while giving up the connotation (the goose root and the rundown, pejorative-augmentative flavor), which the optional note restores rather than the name itself.

Маслоцентр.finding: Маслоцентр was the All-Russian (later All-Union) Union of Dairy Cooperation, the NEP-era apex cooperative that collected, graded, and marketed peasant-made butter, founded around 1924 and active through the early 1930s. Butter was a major Soviet hard-currency export in the 1920s, so this was a real and important trust, not a joke invented for the novel. To a 1928 reader the name was one of the era's stock acronymic agencies (масло + центр, 'butter + centre'), instantly recognisable as bureaucratic NEP-speak; Ilf and Petrov deploy it deadpan for exactly that flat institutional comedy. A literal 'Oil Centre' misreads масло as petroleum; the referent is dairy butter.
Маслоцентр.note_for_reader: Маслоцентр: the All-Russian Union of Dairy Cooperation, the NEP-era trust that collected and exported Soviet butter; масло here is dairy butter, not oil.
Маслоцентр.rationale: I kept denotation (butter, a central cooperative body) and the bureaucratic-acronym register that made a Russian reader smile; I gave up the compact one-word punch of the original acronym, spelling the institution out instead, and the English keeps a parenthetical transliteration to signal it is a proper NEP agency name.

Голубой воришка.finding: Chapter epithet for Alexander Yakovlevich ('Alchen'), the shamefaced supply-manager of the 2nd Stargorod social-security home who pilfers everything and blushes as he does it. 'Голубой' here is not the colour blue and not the modern slang for 'gay'; it is the older poetic sense derived from голубь (dove) meaning meek, mild, gentle, innocent-romantic — used ironically for a man whose whole being protests against theft yet who cannot stop stealing. The diminutive воришка marks him as a petty, sneaking pilferer, not a real criminal, and the pairing is affectionately mocking. The phrase became a Russian catchphrase for a timid, blushing embezzler. The classic English translation renders the chapter title 'The Bashful Chiseller'.
Голубой воришка.note_for_reader: 'Голубой' here is the archaic sense 'dove-gentle, meek', not the colour or the modern slang; the classic English version titles the chapter 'The Bashful Chiseller'.
Голубой воришка.rationale: All three keep the connotation (shame-faced meekness) and the petty-pilferer register of the diminutive воришка — Japanese こそ泥 catches the sneaking pilferer best; they give up the buried голубой=dove/innocent literal layer, which no single target word carries without a note.

Заседание продолжается.finding: Ostap Bender's recurring catchphrase in The Twelve Chairs (Ilf and Petrov, 1928), usually in its full mock-solemn form 'Заседание продолжается, господа присяжные заседатели!' ('The session is in progress, gentlemen of the jury!'). The con man adopts the pompous formula of a courtroom or committee chairman to lend false gravity to ordinary schemes, most famously while chairing the fake conspiratorial 'Union of Sword and Ploughshare'; the joke is the register, not the content. It long ago became a Russian catchphrase for 'the show goes on / business as usual.' The two standard literary translations resolve the pun toward the judicial reading (господа присяжные заседатели = the jury): the widely circulated English version renders it 'The hearing is continued,' and the Chinese edition's editor binds it as '庭审继续进行' (the court hearing continues). I found no Durov/VKontakte-specific rendering of this exact phrase — that association is a distractor; the grounded renderings are literary.
Заседание продолжается.note_for_reader: Ostap apes a courtroom chairman's formula; the mock-solemn judicial register, not the literal 'meeting', is the joke.
Заседание продолжается.rationale: Bound the established literary renderings, keeping denotation and the mock-solemn judicial register that carries the humor across all three languages; gave up the neutral 'meeting/session' wording of the drafts, which loses the courtroom pomposity the joke depends on.

Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.finding: A principal character of Ilf and Petrov's 1928 satire The Twelve Chairs: a former marshal of the nobility (предводитель дворянства) reduced under Soviet rule to a registry-office clerk, who joins the con man Ostap Bender to hunt jewels his mother-in-law sewed into a dining chair. To a Russian reader the tripartite name+patronymic+surname signals pre-revolutionary gentry gravitas that the deadpan narration constantly deflates; the surname derives from воробей ('sparrow'), a small comic bird, and he is mockingly nicknamed 'Киса' (Kisa, 'pussycat'). Existing English versions (Richardson; the Northwestern/Anne O. Fisher edition) keep the full transliterated name; Chinese and Japanese editions likewise transliterate rather than translate it.

При наличии отсутствия.finding: A verbal tic of Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the self-important Stargorod locksmith-intellectual in Ilf and Petrov's 'Twelve Chairs' (1928); his signature line is 'При наличии отсутствия пропитанных шпал это будет не трамвай, а одно горе' ('given the presence of an absence of impregnated sleepers...'), and his parrot later parrots the phrase back. It is an oxymoron: 'при наличии' (given the availability of) is welded to 'отсутствия' (of an absence), so the officialese cancels itself. It reads as pompous Soviet bureaucratic filler that sounds authoritative while meaning nothing, and it became a proverbial Russian tag for self-contradictory pseudo-official gibberish.

Мельстрой.finding: Мельстрой was a real Soviet trust for mill and grain-elevator construction (мельничное строительство), organized in the mid-1920s as a state joint-stock company and later the All-Union State Trust 'Мельстрой', with regional offices (Middle Volga/Samara 1925-1930, later Tomsk and Molotov). In Двенадцать стульев it appears as flavour, not a real player: in the Stargorod tramway-opening chapter its trucks, together with those of Старкомхоз, are the municipal vehicles pressed into carrying the crowd of children. For a 1928 reader the word read as one more clipped NEP-era institutional acronym of the Старкомхоз/Мосдрев type: instantly recognizable in shape as a Soviet trust, faintly comic in its bureaucratic compression, but carrying no plot weight beyond local colour. It must be handled as a coined trust-name of the same class as Старкомхоз, transliterated with a one-time gloss rather than freshly invented.

Виктор Михайлович Полесов.finding: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov is a fictional character in Ilf and Petrov's 'The Twelve Chairs' (1928): a Stargorod slesar-intelligent ('locksmith/mechanic-intellectual'), a self-taught jack-of-all-trades and 'kustar-odinochka s motorom' who leaves paid Starkomkhoz jobs unfinished while meddling loudly in everyone else's business. A nostalgic anti-Soviet grumbler, he is recruited by Ostap Bender into the sham conspiracy 'Union of Sword and Ploughshare.' The name itself carries no wordplay; the comedy sits in his epithet and behaviour, not the name. Published English translations render him 'Victor Mikhailovich Polesov'; the surname Polesov is a plain transliteration with no established semantic gloss in Chinese or Japanese coverage.

Виктор Михайлович Полесов.rationale: A personal name with no internal pun, so all three targets transliterate: denotation (one identifiable person, given-name+patronymic+surname) is fully preserved, while the character's comic connotation is carried by his epithet 'locksmith-intellectual' in the surrounding text, not the name.

«Нимфа».finding: «Нимфа» (the Nymph) is the trade name of the rival coffin-maker's shop in Stargorod that infuriates the undertaker Bezenchuk in the opening chapters of Ilf and Petrov's «Двенадцать стульев» (1928); its silver-trimmed coffins glitter behind wavy green glass and it is run by three co-owners whom the text calls 'the Nymphs'. The comedy is the incongruity of a grandiose, faintly risqué classical name — a naked water-nymph — hung over a funeral parlour, and Bezenchuk sneers that the Nymph cannot really 'give goods' («разве ж он товар дает»). The word functions strictly as a proper business name, not a mythological allusion, so it must stay quoted and consistent. Published translations keep it: English 'the Nymph', Chinese '仙女' (chapter one is titled «别津丘克与"仙女"»), Japanese as the katakana transliteration ニンフ.
«Нимфа».note_for_reader: «Нимфа» is a shop name — the pretentiously classical brand of Bezenchuk's rival coffin business, not a reference to a mythological nymph.
«Нимфа».rationale: English keeps both denotation and the pretentious-classical connotation because 'Nymph' exists as a word; Chinese '仙女' keeps the incongruous beautiful-maiden connotation and the joke of a lovely name on a coffin shop but trades the Greek water-nymph for a native celestial fairy; Japanese katakana ニンフ preserves the foreign classical denotation while muting the risqué overtone. All three keep the quotes so it reads as a brand, not myth.

Клавдия Ивановна.finding: Claudia (Klavdia) Ivanovna Petukhova is the fictional mother-in-law (тёща) of Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928); on her deathbed she confesses she sewed the family diamonds into one of twelve dining chairs to hide them from the revolution. She is addressed by first name plus patronymic, the Russian neutral-respectful form, and referred to structurally as 'тёща'. The Durov/VKontakte guidance in the task template is a boilerplate mismatch and does not apply to this literary character. The long-standing English translation (John Richardson) anglicises her as 'Claudia Ivanovna', which the task's instruction to prefer an established rendering favours over the novel 'Klavdia Ivanovna'.

Клавдия Ивановна.note_for_reader: Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law (тёща); the chair diamonds are her secret.
Клавдия Ивановна.rationale: Transliteration keeps denotation and the polite name+patronymic register; it gives up the internal comic weight of being 'the тёща', which the narration must carry. English follows the established Richardson spelling; zh/ja use standard phonetic transliterations.

гривенник.finding: Гривенник is the everyday Russian name for a ten-kopeck coin (1/10 ruble). The word descends from the medieval гривна and long outlived the imperial silver гривенник, surviving as colloquial speech through the Soviet era, so in the 1920s of Двенадцать стульев it is not a formal denomination but the ordinary way ordinary people named small change. In the novel it is genuinely small money: tourists drop гривенники as an entrance fee, and the yardman's grievance is the lost nightly gate tip from tenants coming home late. It reads to a Russian as a specific, homely small coin, not as an abstract 'ten kopecks'.
гривенник.rationale: All three keep the denotation and the 'small Russian coin' connotation by naming kopecks rather than localizing to dime/penny; English 'piece' and Japanese 玉 recover some of the coin's homely colloquial ring, while the Chinese 硬币 stays neutral, giving up register for clarity.

Тихон.finding: Тихон is a recurring minor character in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928): the drunken yardman (dvornik) of Vorobyaninov's former mansion in Stargorod, a pre-revolutionary servant who was loyal to his old master and is plied with drink by Bender so he will not betray them. The word is an ordinary Russian male given name (from Greek Tychon, 'lucky/hitting the mark'), old-fashioned and faintly rustic, with churchly overtones — it is also the name of Patriarch Tikhon — but in the novel it functions purely as a proper name, not as a pun. Existing English, Chinese and Japanese editions render it by straight phonetic transliteration (the Japanese translation is 江川卓's 十二の椅子).
Тихон.rationale: Keep denotation and stable spelling by standard transliteration; give up the name's faint churchly/rustic connotation, which is inaudible to the target reader and carries no plot weight.

Перелешинский переулок.finding: A street name in the fictional provincial town of Stargorod in Ilf and Petrov's Twelve Chairs, not a real Moscow lane. In the chapter 'The Locksmith, the Parrot and the Fortune-teller' (Ch. X), house No. 7 in Perelешинский переулок is the home of the fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna Bour, later a meeting place of the mock-conspiratorial 'Union of Sword and Ploughshare.' The name is a plausible pre-revolutionary street name derived from a surname (Перелешин); to a Russian reader it reads as an ordinary, faintly old-regime provincial address with no special meaning beyond local color. (The prompt's note about Durov and VKontakte, c.2013, does not apply to this term and was disregarded.)

Перелешинский переулок.rationale: Preserved denotation (a recognizable proper street name) and the neutral narrative register by transliterating the opaque name and rendering переулок consistently as the generic 'lane'; gave up the faint pre-revolutionary/provincial coloring of the -ский name, which no target reader would hear. For zh I chose 巷 over the proposed 胡同 to avoid importing a distinctly Beijing flavor into a Russian town.

«Сорбонна».finding: «Сорбонна» is the name of a shabby provincial hotel (гостиница / меблированные комнаты) in Stargorod where Ostap Bender and Vorobyaninov lodge in Ilf and Petrov's Двенадцать стульев (1928); the text styles it in guillemets and shows its shuttle-wagon and corridors ('Из гостиничной линейки с вывеской «Сорбонна»…'). The comedy is pure incongruity: a squalid backwater inn grandly named after the celebrated Paris university, a stock satirical jab at provincial pretensions to metropolitan grandeur that a 1928 Russian reader caught instantly. It is a proper name, not the real Sorbonne, and the reference is globally recognizable, so it carries across languages.
«Сорбонна».note_for_reader: A grubby provincial hotel grandly named after the Paris university.
«Сорбонна».rationale: Kept denotation (the name Sorbonne) and connotation (the ironic incongruity, which survives because the Paris Sorbonne is known everywhere), with quotes preserving the sign; used the established equivalents 索邦 / ソルボンヌ. Gave up only the specifically Russian flavour of provincial swagger, which the brief note restores.

Альхен.finding: Альхен is the hypocoristic (pet-name) form of Александр Яковлевич, the mortifyingly polite manager of the No. 2 Home for the Aged in Stargorod, a compulsive petty thief the narrators famously dub the 'голубой воришка' (sky-blue/bashful little thief). The name pairs with his wife's: he calls her Сашхен, she calls him Альхен, a mock-tender German-flavoured diminutive (‑chen) that mirrors their genteel embarrassment. For a Russian reader the word is instantly domestic and comic, and it is distinct from his formal 'Александр Яковлевич'. Established English translations differ: Richardson (1961) writes 'Alchen' ('he used to call her Sashchen, and she used to call him Alchen'); Fisher (2011) writes 'Alkhen'. Chinese editions render it 阿尔兴; the Japanese translation is Egawa Taku's.
Альхен.note_for_reader: Alkhen is a pet form of Alexander; his wife is Sashkhen — mock-tender domestic diminutives.
Альхен.rationale: Bound the established phonetic transliterations, keeping denotation and a stable form distinct from the formal 'Alexander Yakovlevich'; 'Alkhen' keeps the Russian /x/ audible (over Richardson's softer 'Alchen'). We give up the ‑chen diminutive's tender-comic connotation, which no target script can carry, hence the short note.

Воробьянинов.finding: Surname of Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the ex-marshal of the nobility (predvoditel dvoryanstva) and hapless treasure-hunter of Ilf and Petrov's 'The Twelve Chairs' (1928), nicknamed Kisa. To a Russian reader the name is transparently built on воробей ('sparrow'), lending a faintly comic, diminutive undertone that deflates his lordly pretensions, but functionally it reads as an ordinary gentry surname. The fixed problem is transliteration: the -ья- (b'ya) cluster must render as one stable form across the book. English coverage and the Fisher translation use 'Vorobyaninov'; Chinese coverage (Baidu Baike, Douban) settles on 沃洛比亚尼诺夫; Japanese editions use ヴォロビヤニノフ.
Воробьянинов.rationale: Each rendering keeps denotation (a fixed, unambiguous name for the character) and register (a plain surname) but gives up the buried воробей/'sparrow' connotation, which no transliteration can carry; zh follows the established 沃洛 form over the variant 沃罗.

великий комбинатор.finding: The narrator's recurring mock-heroic epithet for Ostap Bender in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928) and The Golden Calf (1931). великий = 'great/grand', a grandiose elevation; комбинатор = one who runs 'комбинации' (schemes, deals, angles) — a wheeler-dealer/con artist, not the logician's 'combinator'. The phrase is ironic: it crowns a charming small-time swindler with a swindler's grandeur, and it became a fixed Russian catchphrase for a resourceful schemer. English translations diverge — John Richardson's classic version renders it 'the smooth operator', while Wikipedia and others gloss it 'the great schemer/great combinator'; there is no single uncontested rendering.
великий комбинатор.note_for_reader: Ostap Bender's standing mock-heroic epithet; John Richardson's classic English translation renders it 'the smooth operator.'
великий комбинатор.rationale: Keeps the mock-solemn grandeur of великий and the calculating-schemer denotation, and holds all three languages parallel (grand + strategist) for side-by-side reading; gives up the wheeler-dealer/con-artist flavor of комбинатор that Richardson's colloquial 'smooth operator' catches.

Остап.finding: Ostap Bender is the young con man and central rogue of Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928) and its sequel The Golden Calf; the given name Остап is the East Slavic/Ukrainian form of Eustathius, marking him as a rootless southerner (he is nicknamed the 'smooth operator' and calls himself son of a Turkish subject). For a Russian reader the name is instantly iconic, carrying charm, wit, and swindling rather than any menace. Published translations fix the first name as Ostap in English, 奥斯塔普 in Chinese (surname 本德尔), and オスタップ in Japanese (Egawa Taku's オスタップ・ベンデル); these are the standard, non-contested transliterations of the given name even though the surname Бендер varies more.
Остап.rationale: Preserves denotation and the established published transliteration in all three languages (matching the surname Bender / 本德尔 / ベンデル); gives up the Ukrainian-southerner connotation of the given name, which no transliteration can carry without a note.

дворник.finding: In pre- and early-Soviet Russia the дворник was the live-in yard-and-building keeper attached to a specific apartment house, not a modern cleaner. Beyond sweeping the courtyard and clearing snow, he was a figure of authority: he watched the tenants, kept order, witnessed searches, and registered arrivals for the police. Crucially, he locked the building's gate (ворота) at night and held the key, so a tenant who came home late had to knock and tip him a copeck or гривенник to be let in — a small but reliable perk on top of a decent wage. That gate-keeping livelihood, now vanished, is exactly what makes the lost гривенники a joke a 1928 reader caught at once.
дворник.note_for_reader: The дворник locked the building's gate at night and earned a small tip for letting late tenants in.
дворник.rationale: All three renderings keep the gate-keeping role and neutral register that make the tip joke work; they give up the literal 'yard/sweeper' denotation of двор. English 'caretaker' is chosen over 'yardman', which misreads as a farm/stable hand and loses the building-and-gate authority.

губплан.finding: Губплан is the clipped acronym for губернская плановая комиссия, the provincial (guberniya-level) planning commission set up from 1921 under the new Gosplan system as a local economic-planning body attached to the provincial executive committee (губисполком/губЭКОСО). It drafted and coordinated economic plans for its guberniya and reported up the Gosplan chain. These commissions were short-lived: as guberniyas were replaced by oblasts and krais in the mid-1920s administrative reform, the губплан gave way to the областная плановая комиссия (облплан). For a Soviet reader of 1928 it carried no exotic weight — it was one of the grey, faintly comic NEP-era bureaucratic acronyms, an anonymous provincial office, exactly the kind of clipped institutional name the novel keeps deadpan.

rendering.ja: 県計画委員会（グブプラン）

губплан.note_for_reader: A 1920s provincial branch of the Soviet central-planning apparatus (Gosplan).
губплан.rationale: Kept denotation and the bureaucratic register by glossing the office transparently; gave up the compact acronym-flavour that a Russian reader hears, restored only as a parenthetical transliteration.

дворницкая.finding: The дворницкая is the lodge or room occupied by the дворник (yardman/caretaker), the man who swept the courtyard, opened and locked the gate, cleared snow, and knew every resident. In pre-revolutionary and NEP-era buildings it was typically a small semi-basement or ground-floor room off the courtyard, entered from under the archway. The дворник was not just a cleaner but a quasi-official gatekeeper and police informant, the de facto master of the building, so the space carried an air of low-status but knowing, always-watching authority. In the novel it is Tikhon's room in Vorobyaninov's former mansion, where Bender and Vorobyaninov first camp out; dictionaries gloss дворницкая plainly as 'the yardman's room'.
дворницкая.note_for_reader: A дворник was a live-in yardman: sweeper, gatekeeper, and semi-official watchman/informant for the building.
дворницкая.rationale: Keeps denotation (the caretaker's own room) and neutral register; gives up the connotation of the дворник as gatekeeper-informant, which no single word carries, so the note supplies it.

брандмейстер.finding: Брандмейстер (from German Brandmeister, 'fire master') was the chief of a municipal fire brigade in Imperial Russia and the early USSR, a fire-service officer who reported to the брандмайор (the city-wide fire chief). Originally a police-department post, it was a real rank still in use in the 1920s but carried an old-regime, German-derived officialese flavor by 1928. In The Twelve Chairs the брандмейстер appears at civic gatherings in Stargorod as a figure of provincial bureaucratic pomp; the word itself reads as slightly antiquated officialdom. Russian and Japanese reference sources gloss it plainly as the head of a fire brigade (начальник пожарной команды).
брандмейстер.rationale: Keeps the denotation (head of the town fire brigade) and a plainly formal register that all three target readers understand without a footnote; gives up the German-derived, faintly antiquated old-regime officialese connotation, which no everyday modern equivalent preserves.

вдова Грицацуева.finding: Madame Gritsatsuyeva is a secondary character in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928): a plump, adoring NEP-era shopkeeper widow whom the con man Ostap Bender marries only to get one of the twelve chairs, then abandons the next morning, taking the chair and a gilt tea-strainer. The comic effect for a Russian reader comes from the surname, which sounds exaggeratedly Ukrainian/provincial, paired with Bender's mock-poetic line about her, 'знойная женщина — мечта поэта' (a sultry woman, a poet's dream), which became a catchphrase; the name itself became a byword for a naive, grasping provincial wife. 'Вдова' here is her situation, not a rank or title. The task's instruction to check Durov/VKontakte coverage does not apply — this is a fictional character, not the internet figure — so I researched the novel directly.

rendering.ja: 未亡人グリツァツーエワ

вдова Грицацуева.note_for_reader: The surname sounds comically provincial-Ukrainian to a Russian ear; 'widow' is her situation, not a title.
вдова Грицацуева.rationale: Kept denotation and stable transliteration in all three, treating 'widow' as a common-noun descriptor she can lose, not a rank; gave up the surname's built-in comic Ukrainian ring, which no transliteration carries without the one-line note.

Остап Бендер.finding: Ostap Bender is the central con man of Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928) and its sequel The Little Golden Calf (1931), a charming, quick-witted swindler who styles himself a 'great schemer' (великий комбинатор). For a Russian reader the name is instantly recognizable, and many of his lines became proverbs; the surname reads as faintly exotic (non-Russian, vaguely southern/Odessan), reinforcing his rootless-adventurer aura. Existing English, Japanese and Chinese coverage all transliterate the name rather than translating it: English 'Ostap Bender' (Wikipedia, published translations), Japanese オスタップ・ベンデル (Japanese editions of 十二の椅子; RBTH Japan), Chinese 奥斯塔普·本德尔 (Chinese editions of 《十二把椅子》, Douban).

rendering.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

Остап Бендер.rationale: As a proper name, transliteration preserves denotation (the fixed, book-wide identity and stress) and matches the established renderings in each language; it gives up the faint 'foreign/southern surname' connotation a Russian reader hears, which no phonetic form can carry without a note.

делопроизводитель загса.finding: Делопроизводитель is a formal Soviet clerical title (records/office clerk), and ЗАГС is the acronym for the civil-registry office (отдел записи актов гражданского состояния) that logs births, marriages and deaths. In Двенадцать стульев this is the day job of Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov in the town of N./Stargorod: a former marshal of the nobility now sitting at the deaths-and-marriages desk. The comedy is the drop in status, not the words themselves — a grandee reduced to a petty Soviet paper-pusher. The 1961 Richardson/Salis English version renders it descriptively ('he worked in the registry office... deaths-and-marriages desk') rather than transliterating the acronym.

rendering.en: records clerk at the civil-registry office (ZAGS)

делопроизводитель загса.note_for_reader: ZAGS = the Soviet civil-registry office for births, marriages and deaths.
делопроизводитель загса.rationale: Keeps denotation (a lowly civil-registry clerk) and the humble bureaucratic register that sets up the ex-noble joke; gives up carrying the acronym's Soviet flavour unglossed, so ZAGS is retained once in parentheses instead of left bare.

брильянты.finding: Брильянты is a colloquial/older-spelling variant of бриллианты, meaning cut and polished diamonds (brilliant-cut gemstones), as opposed to алмаз, the rough uncut mineral. In the novel these are Madame Petukhova's finished jewelry stones, sewn into one dining chair — the book-long prize. To a 1928 Russian reader the word denoted specifically faceted jewel-quality diamonds (fabulous, sellable wealth), not raw stone; the -иль- spelling carries a faintly old-fashioned, everyday-speech flavor. English translations fix it as 'diamonds' (the chapter Бриллиантовый дым is rendered 'Diamond Smoke').
брильянты.rationale: Keeps denotation (cut jewel-quality diamonds, the fixed macguffin) and neutral register; gives up the faint old-fashioned/colloquial coloring of the -иль- spelling, which no single target word can carry. 'Diamonds'/钻石/ダイヤモンド each name the finished gem, not the raw mineral (алмаз/金刚石/金剛石), so the cut-stone specificity survives.

концессионеры.finding: The word derives from концессия, the NEP-era term for a state-granted business concession under which foreign and private firms were licensed to run enterprises. Early in the novel Ostap Bender proposes that he and Vorobyaninov form a 'concession' to recover the jewels sewn into a chair, complete with a fixed profit split, and thereafter the narrator recurrently and mock-solemnly labels the pair 'концессионеры.' The joke is that two men with no legal standing dress an illicit treasure hunt in the dignified, official vocabulary of a sanctioned NEP venture; the epithet is deadpan and ironic and became one of the book's running gags. A Russian reader caught both the NEP-concession allusion and the mock-official pomposity. (The task's 'Durov/VKontakte, ~2013' framing is a template mismatch; this is the 1928 Ilf & Petrov term.)
концессионеры.note_for_reader: 'Concession' echoes the NEP-era state business concessions (концессии); the narrator dignifies the pair's treasure hunt with that legal-commercial word.
концессионеры.rationale: English 'the concessionaires' keeps all three — the concession denotation, the mock-solemn irony, and the formal-business register — and matches the established translations. Chinese 特许权合伙人 keeps denotation and register but softens the recurring mock-solemn punch; Japanese 利権コンビ keeps the ironic self-interest connotation (利権) but trades formal register for the comic transparency of コンビ ('duo').

архивариус.finding: Архивариус is a Latinate borrowing (Lat. archivarius, via obsolete German, entering Russian under Peter I) for the keeper or head of an archive. Until the early 20th c. it specifically denoted the official in charge of an archive, distinct from the plainer архивист that has since displaced it; today it survives as a grand-sounding, dated word for an archive clerk. Applied to Varfolomey Korobeinikov, a petty ex-clerk of the town-governor's chancery who now hoards requisition orders in a shabby back room, the pompous old title is deliberately oversized for the man and his job, which is the joke. The near-synonym архиварий is marked устар. (obsolete); the word itself reads as bookish and old-fashioned rather than colloquial.
архивариус.note_for_reader: The word is a pompous, archaic term for what is really a lowly archive clerk; the grandeur is the joke.
архивариус.rationale: Kept connotation and register (mock-solemn, dated grandeur) over the flattest denotation: 'archivarius', 总管, and 官 each inflate a humble records-keeper, where plain archivist/档案保管员/保管係 would give up the comedy.

гробовых дел мастер.finding: It is the mock-grandiose sign/title of Bezenchuk, the shabby coffin-maker in Chapter 1 of The Twelve Chairs. It is built on the archaic Russian guild-craft formula '<X> дел мастер' ('master of the <X> craft'), whose most familiar member is 'золотых дел мастер' = goldsmith/master jeweller; substituting 'гробовых' (of coffins) into that dignified formula is the joke, dressing a provincial undertaker in a lofty pre-revolutionary artisan title. To a 1928 (and 2013) Russian reader the pattern instantly reads as old-fashioned, bookish and pompous, which is why plain 'undertaker' loses the humour. The classic Richardson English translation flattens it to just 'undertaker'; the archaic guild ring is the half that must be carried.
гробовых дел мастер.note_for_reader: Mimics the old guild title 'master of the goldsmith's craft' — a pompous professional label pinned on a small-town coffin-maker.
гробовых дел мастер.rationale: Each rendering keeps the denotation (coffin-maker) and the connotation/register of a stiff archaic guild title (en 'master of the ... craft', zh 大师傅, ja 親方) that echoes 'goldsmith'; what is given up is the everyday brevity and naturalness of plain 'undertaker'.

губисполком.finding: Contraction of губернский исполнительный комитет — the executive committee elected by a provincial (guberniya) congress of soviets, and the standing administrative organ that actually ran a gubernia between 1917 and the 1929–30 abolition of gubernias in favour of oblasts and raions. Its chairman was the region's top official, roughly a Soviet governor, which is why he 'opens the line'. The word is itself a clipped 1920s Soviet acronym-portmanteau, exactly the terse new officialese Ilf and Petrov mock; a 1928 reader heard both 'the local seat of Soviet power' and the faint absurdity of compressed bureaucratic newspeak.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ロシア・ソビエト連邦社会主義共和国の行政区画

rendering.en: the gubispolkom (the provincial soviet executive committee)

губисполком.note_for_reader: Gubispolkom = the elected executive body running a Russian province (guberniya) in the early Soviet years; its chairman was effectively the regional governor.
губисполком.rationale: English keeps denotation and the period connotation (transliterated acronym + gloss) but gives up the term's clipped brevity; Chinese and Japanese keep denotation and neutral-official register but give up both the acronym compression and the era-specific flavour, which the note restores.

батюшка.finding: Батюшка is the warm, folksy, diminutive-affectionate form of address for a Russian Orthodox parish priest ('little father'), colloquial and intimate rather than the formal 'отец Фёдор' or the neutral 'священник'. Dictionaries mark it colloquial and affectionate; it can also be a coaxing term of endearment ('my dear fellow'). In Двенадцать стульев the register is the point: the sweet, deferential-sounding address is aimed at Father Fyodor mockingly, so the tone is affectionate on the surface and ironic underneath. A 1928 Russian reader heard it as pious-familiar church-village speech being used with a straight comic face.
батюшка.rationale: Kept denotation (a priest) and the mock-sweet/ironic register; 'Father dear', 神父大人 and 神父さま each add exaggerated warmth or deference so the irony lands. Gave up exact confessional accuracy (神父 reads Catholic, not the precise Orthodox 司祭) and the specifically folksy-diminutive flavor, trading it for mock-reverence the general reader catches without a note.

красный уголок.finding: A красный уголок was a small room or set-aside corner in every Soviet workplace, barracks, dormitory, school and collective farm, reserved for political education: collective newspaper readings, literacy and 'political-literacy' classes, party and union meetings, agitprop displays, and an obligatory portrait of Lenin draped in red cloth. It arose in the early 1920s (first in Red Army barracks, c.1921); after Lenin's death in 1924 many were renamed ленинский уголок / ленинская комната ('Lenin corner/room'). The name puns on the pre-revolutionary красный угол, the 'beautiful/holy corner' where a peasant household hung its icons, so the Bolshevik version pointedly installed Lenin's image where the icon had been. To a 1928 reader it was an instantly recognizable, faintly comic, official-and-obligatory fixture of Soviet institutional life; trade unions ran hundreds of thousands of them.

rendering.en: the Lenin corner (the compulsory political reading-room)

красный уголок.note_for_reader: The name puns on the красный угол, the Orthodox 'icon corner' of a peasant home; Lenin's portrait now hangs where the icon did.
красный уголок.rationale: Kept the denotation (a mandatory Soviet political-education room) and its official, mock-solemn connotation via a glossed term; gave up the buried pun on the Orthodox icon-corner, which the note carries instead.

господа присяжные заседатели.finding: A fixed courtroom form of address, literally 'gentlemen of the jury', from the Imperial Russian jury trial that ran 1864-1918 before the Soviets abolished it in favour of 'people's assessors'. By the NEP years of the novel it was an anachronism, redolent of pre-revolutionary legal oratory, which is why Ostap Bender's deadpan use of it is comic: he drops the solemn legal-address cliche into non-courtroom situations (famously 'Лёд тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели!' and here into a fund-raising appeal for homeless children). It became one of the book's proverbial catchphrases; a Russian reader hears a con man aping a lawyer's mock-solemn address to a jury that is not there.
господа присяжные заседатели.note_for_reader: A stock courtroom address ('gentlemen of the jury') Ostap deploys where there is no jury, for mock-solemn effect.
господа присяжные заседатели.rationale: Kept the set legal-address denotation and formal register in all three so the incongruity of an oration to an absent jury lands; gave up the specifically Imperial-Russian, pre-1918 flavour, which no target reader hears in 'jury' without a note (ja 諸君 and zh 先生们 preserve the mock-solemn 'gentlemen' address).

допр.finding: ДОПР = Дом принудительных работ, 'house of forced labor,' an early-Soviet local place of detention with a compulsory-labor regime, run by the NKVD in the 1920s (predating the GULAG camp system). It was an ordinary town jail/lockup where short and medium sentences were served, not a distant camp. By 1928 the acronym had passed into everyday speech as a routine, unglamorous word for 'the clink'; part of the deadpan comedy is exactly the Soviet mania for abbreviations. In the novel it also yields Kislyarsky's 'допровская корзинка' — a bag kept packed against the day one is jailed. I could not confirm a single established published English/Chinese/Japanese rendering of the bare acronym.
допр.note_for_reader: DOPR = Dom prinuditelnykh rabot, an NKVD-run 1920s town jail with a labor regime; the joke is partly the Soviet love of acronyms.
допр.rationale: Keeps denotation (a forced-labor jail) and the acronym-comedy connotation by preserving the Latin acronym DOPR plus a short gloss; gives up the fact that a 1928 reader heard it as ordinary slang, only partly restored by the gloss. I prefer bare 'DOPR' over the phonetic ドプル / 多普尔, which read to a CJK technical reader as an opaque foreign proper name rather than an acronym.

отец Федор.finding: Отец Федор is Father Fyodor Ivanovich Vostrikov, the Russian Orthodox priest in Ilf and Petrov's Двенадцать стульев (1928) who hears the dying Madame Petukhova's confession, learns of the jewels sewn into one chair, and becomes Vorobyaninov and Bender's secret rival in the hunt. 'Отец' here is the clerical vocative title 'Father', not the kinship word; it marks him as clergy and carries the mock-solemn religious register the narrators play against his greed and comic schemes. In existing coverage the name is rendered established: English translations and Wikipedia use 'Father Fyodor', Chinese editions use 费奥多尔神父, and the Japanese tradition (Egawa Taku's 十二の椅子) and general usage give フョードル神父. Note that 神父 (shinpu/shenfu) is the widely-understood 'priest/Father' term though it reads Catholic; the strictly Orthodox term would be 司祭, but 神父 is what a non-specialist reader parses instantly.
отец Федор.note_for_reader: "Father" is his clerical title: he is an Orthodox priest, not a relative.
отец Федор.rationale: Keeps denotation (the named priest) and the clerical register via 'Father'/神父/神父, matching the established renderings; gives up the strictly Orthodox nuance (神父 reads Catholic rather than 司祭) for the sake of immediate legibility to a non-specialist reader.

конгениально.finding: Конгениальный is a real Russian bookish borrowing (via German kongenial, from Latin con- + genius) meaning 'kindred in spirit, matching in talent/genius WITH someone or something' — a relational word, not a standalone 'brilliant'. Ostap Bender flings it out as an exclamation, 'Это конгениально!', to crown a clever idea as sheer genius, misusing the learned word by dropping its relational sense and treating it as a fancy synonym for гениально ('brilliant'). The comedy is in the showy, half-understood Latinate flourish coming from a self-taught con man, not in the plain praise it conveys; the line became one of his catchphrases. A Russian reader hears both the flattery and the pretension at once.
конгениально.note_for_reader: Ostap misuses a fancy word: 'congenial' (kindred in spirit) stands in for 'sheer genius'.
конгениально.rationale: I keep register (showy, misapplied learned word) and connotation (grand praise); English preserves the Latinate misuse via 'congenial', which shares the genius root, at some cost to plain denotation, so the one-line note restores meaning. Chinese/Japanese cannot echo 'congenial' idiomatically, so they keep denotation and register ('a work of genius' / 'truly genius') and lean on the note for the misuse.

жилотдел.finding: Жилотдел is a clipped compound for жилищный отдел, the housing subdepartment of a local soviet's executive committee (исполком) in the early Soviet/NEP years. It managed municipal housing and the furniture requisitioned from private homes after 1918; in the novel its archive of distribution orders (ордера) is the paper trail showing where the confiscated Vorobyaninov chairs were sent. To a 1928 Russian reader the word carried the flavour of the era's ubiquitous truncated bureaucratic coinages (жилотдел, собес, губсоцстрах) — a plain municipal office whose comedy lies in its ugly clipped Soviet name, not in any hidden meaning.
жилотдел.rationale: Transparent department names keep the denotation and the drab bureaucratic register in all three languages; what is given up is the connotation of the clipped Soviet acronym-coinage, which no plain rendering can carry without a note the reader does not need here.

матушка.finding: In Russian Orthodox usage матушка is the customary form of address and reference for a married priest's wife (the parallel to батюшка for the priest himself); Orthodox parish clergy of the white clergy marry before ordination, so a priest having a wife is normal, not scandalous. The word is literally an affectionate diminutive of 'mother' ('little mother'), and its force is domestic, warm and deferential rather than literal maternity. In The Twelve Chairs it belongs to Father Fyodor's church-and-provincial register: he uses it of/to his wife, and the humour rides on that pious, old-fashioned domesticity against the treasure hunt. A non-specialist reader hears only 'mother/mummy' unless the ecclesiastical sense is supplied.
матушка.note_for_reader: Matushka: Orthodox parish priests marry; the word is the affectionate title for the priest's wife, not 'mother'.
матушка.rationale: Each rendering keeps the denotation (the priest's wife) and the correct ecclesiastical frame, but gives up the affectionate diminutive connotation and the vocative warmth of матушка; the one-line note restores the sense that would otherwise read as literal 'mother'.

милиционер.finding: Милиционер is a member of the Soviet милиция, the ordinary civil police. The Bolsheviks (following the 1917 Provisional Government) named the force 'militia' to distance it from the tsarist полиция and evoke a people's self-policing body, but by 1928 it denoted plain uniformed police, not a paramilitary or citizen levy. In the scene he simply marches a brawling yardman to the district station (район). Russia kept the name until the 2011 reform renamed the force полиция; for a Russian reader the word reads as everyday 'cop', with faint Soviet coloring.
милиционер.note_for_reader: In the USSR the ordinary police were called the 'militia' (militsiya) - civil police, no paramilitary sense.
милиционер.rationale: In all three I keep denotation (civil police) and neutral register; English gives up the 'militia' coloring to block the paramilitary misread, while Chinese and Japanese 民警 is the established rendering that both means 'police' and preserves the Soviet flavor.

концессия.finding: Under the NEP (1921-1929) a концессия was a formal business grant by which the Soviet state let foreign capital operate mines, forests, oilfields and factories on its territory; it was a live, semi-official economic term a 1928 reader knew from newspapers. In the novel Ostap Bender ironically dignifies the private treasure hunt as a концессия and the two partners as концессионеры, framing their scramble for jewels as a legitimate joint enterprise with negotiated profit shares (Bender's 'sixty per cent'). The joke is the clash between the pompous economic-legal register and the crooked reality. The established English translation renders it 'concession' / 'concessionaires', and the standard economic-history renderings are 租让 in Chinese and 利権 in Japanese.
концессия.note_for_reader: A NEP-era 'concession' was a business grant the Soviet state gave foreign capital; the partners mock-solemnly call their treasure hunt one.
концессия.rationale: Kept denotation (a state-granted business venture) and the mock-formal economic register, which is what makes the irony land and lets 'concessionaires' work for the pair; gave up the specific 1928 resonance with real foreign concessions, which the one-line note supplies.
